# Congruences making `(350892 m^3 - 1) / k` an integer
For each digit size `d = 10, 20, ..., 100` the constants below satisfy:
> if `k ≡ a₁ (mod b₁)` with `0 < k < b₁`, and `m ≡ a₂ (mod b₂)`, then `k` divides `350892 m³ − 1`,
i.e. `(350892 m³ − 1)/k` is an integer.  All four constants have exactly `d` digits
and are **pairwise distinct** — in particular `a₁ ≠ a₂` and `a₁ ≠ b₂`.
Construction: `a₁ = p` is a `d`-digit prime with `p ≡ 2 (mod 3)` (so `x ↦ x³` is a
bijection mod `p`) and `2p < 10^d`; `b₁ = 10^d − 1`, so `k ≡ a₁ (mod b₁)` together with
`0 < k < b₁` pins `k = p`.  The modulus for `m` is `b₂ = 2p`, and `a₂` is the residue in
`(p, 2p)` with `350892 a₂³ ≡ 1 (mod p)`.  Since `p ∣ b₂`, every `m ≡ a₂ (mod b₂)` satisfies
`m ≡ a₂ (mod p)` and hence `p ∣ 350892 m³ − 1`.  The `m`-congruence is unrestricted.
The bounds `0 < k < b₁` cannot be dropped — see `no_unbounded_k_congruence`
in `RequestProject/CubicCongruence.lean`, which proves that no pair of congruences
can force the divisibility for all `k` in an infinite residue class.
Machine-checked statements: `CubicCongruence.integrality_digits_d` (integrality) and
`CubicCongruence.constants_distinct_d` (pairwise distinctness) for each `d`.

- `a₁ = 1000000007`
- `b₁ = 9999999999`
- `a₂ = 1600805382`
- `b₂ = 2000000014`
